title: I'm a Reading Interventionist but I Don't Teach Reading
author: scienceofreadingclassroom
summary: A middle school reading interventionist makes the provocative claim that she does not teach reading -- she teaches knowledge, and reading happens as a result. The piece explains that the students she works with can decode adequately but cannot comprehend what they decode because they lack the background knowledge that comprehension requires. She has redesigned her intervention program entirely around building content knowledge through high-interest social studies texts, using structured discussion, knowledge-building read-alouds, and explicit vocabulary instruction tied to content rather than to generic vocabulary skills. The piece documents what the research on reading comprehension tells us: reading skill is largely knowledge skill, and reading interventions that focus on reading strategies rather than content knowledge are misidentifying the problem. The interventionist describes specific lessons, specific texts, and specific student responses that illustrate the difference between a student who has the decoding but lacks the knowledge and a student who has both.
points: * Students who can decode adequately but cannot comprehend are experiencing a knowledge problem, not a reading strategy problem -- the most effective reading intervention for these students builds content knowledge, not reading skills. * The science of reading shows that reading comprehension is largely determined by background knowledge: a reader understands a text in proportion to how much they already know about the domain the text describes. * Reading interventions that focus on comprehension strategies (main idea, summarizing, inferencing) without building content knowledge are treating the symptom rather than the cause for many struggling middle school readers. * Social studies texts are the interventionist's primary instructional tool because they build the world knowledge that determines comprehension across all subjects -- history, geography, civics, and economics are domains that compound. * Structured discussion and knowledge-building read-alouds are the key pedagogical moves: they allow the teacher to build knowledge faster than independent reading would, and they give students the oral vocabulary they need before they encounter it in text.
quotes: I am a reading interventionist. I am also almost never teaching reading skills. The students who come to me can decode. Most of them can decode quite well. What they cannot do is understand what they've decoded, because they don't know enough about the world to make meaning from text about it.

The research on this is not ambiguous. Reading comprehension is largely knowledge comprehension. A reader who knows a lot about the domain of a text will comprehend that text well. A reader who knows nothing about the domain will comprehend poorly, regardless of how skilled they are at identifying the main idea or making inferences.

When I changed my intervention program from comprehension strategies to content knowledge, my students' comprehension scores went up. This is not a surprise if you've read the research. It is a surprise if you have been trained to think that reading skills are separable from content knowledge. They are not.

The most powerful thing I can do in 45 minutes with a struggling reader is not teach them to make inferences. It is read them a rich text, talk about what it means, connect it to what they already know, and add to what they know. Tomorrow, when they encounter a related text on their own, they will comprehend it better. That is the intervention.

Knowledge builds on knowledge. A student who knows more about history reads historical texts better. A student who reads historical texts better learns more history. The cycle is virtuous if you start it and vicious if you don't.
